It's time to use your first Dolt feature. We're going to make a Dolt commit. A Dolt commit allows you to time travel and see lineage. Make a Dolt commit whenever you want to restore or compare to this point in time.

Dolt exposes version control functionality through a Git-style interface. On the command line, Dolt commands map exactly to their Git equivalent with the targets being tables instead of files. In SQL, Dolt exposes version control read operations as system tables and version control write operations as stored procedures.

Note, a Dolt commit is different than a standard SQL transaction `COMMIT`. In this case, I am running the database with `AUTOCOMMIT` on, so each SQL statement is automatically generating a transaction `COMMIT`. If you want system to generate a Dolt commit for every transaction use the system variable, `@@dolt_transaction_commit`.

Dolt makes operating databases less error prone. You can always back out changes you have in progress or rewind to a known good state. You also have the ability to undo specific commits using `dolt_revert()`. Even if you accidentally run `drop database` on the wrong database, Dolt lets you undo that by calling the `dolt_undrop()` stored procedure.

OrbitDB is a **serverless, distributed, peer-to-peer database**. OrbitDB uses IPFS as its data storage and Libp2p Pubsub to automatically sync databases with peers. It's an eventually consistent database that uses Merkle-CRDTs for conflict-free database writes and merges making OrbitDB an excellent choice for p2p and decentralized apps, blockchain applications and local-first web applications.
- **events**: an immutable (append-only) log with traversable history. Useful for *"latest N"* use cases or as a message queue.
- **documents**: a document database to which JSON documents can be stored and indexed by a specified key. Useful for building search indices or version controlling documents and data.
- **keyvalue**: a key-value database just like your favourite key-value database.
- **keyvalue-indexed**: key-value data indexed in a Level key-value database.

All databases are implemented on top of OrbitDB's OpLog, an immutable, cryptographically verifiable, operation-based conflict-free replicated data structure (CRDT) for distributed systems. OpLog is formalized in the paper Merkle-CRDTs. You can also easily extend OrbitDB by implementing and using a custom data model benefitting from the same properties as the default data models provided by the underlying Merkle-CRDTs.
A Go implementation is developed and maintained by the Berty project at berty/go-orbit-db.
If you want to get up and running with OrbitDB quickly, install and follow the instructions in the @orbitdb/quickstart module.

Editable uses Svedit as its editing engine. This chapter covers the Svedit primitives used to render content, but Svedit's separate API documentation is the reference for schemas, sessions, transactions, transforms, commands, marks, and annotations. Study that API to move beyond adapting Editable's existing patterns and build new editing behavior of your own.

Code blocks are placed with `layout`, like prose, and always keep their text left-aligned. Their `language` and `wrap_lines` are set in a popover above the block, which appears while the caret is in the block or the block is selected. `plain` (the default) leaves highlighting off. Long lines scroll sideways unless `wrap_lines` is on. A copy button sits beside the first line, in a column of its own, so it never covers code. Twinkleplop highlights selected languages in both view and edit mode. Language grammars load on demand, and the native range painter loads only when editing. View rendering awaits its grammar during server rendering and hydration; editing stays plain until the grammar loads. Editing uses native CSS highlight ranges without changing Svedit’s text DOM. Updates are batched to animation frames and pause during IME composition. Blocks exceeding 50,000 UTF-16 code units or 4,000 syntax ranges use plain text editing to keep highlighting work bounded; they still highlight in view mode. Highlighting resumes automatically when the block is shortened. Browsers without the CSS Custom Highlight API retain plain text editing. Supported language ids are listed in src/app/code_languages.ts. Markdown imports preserve supported fence languages and common aliases such as `js`, `ts`, and `sh`. Existing preformatted nodes migrate to plain code blocks.

Annotation nodes must not have registered rendering components. For node arrays, child components receive every covering annotation through their `annotations` prop, and `Node` adds classes such as `anno-comment`, `anno-comment-start`, and `anno-comment-end`. Text annotations remain data-only, so comments or other interactive annotations usually need an overlay. The Svedit API documents selection state, annotation commands, transactions, and rendering integration in full.

Editable runs on any VPS — all you need is Node.js, and the included `Dockerfile` works with any platform that supports Docker (see Deploy to a VPS). The repository ships ready-made for Fly.io, which remains the recommended default: machines scale to zero and wake in well under a second, so a personal site costs next to nothing to run. Install flyctl, then sign in (opens your browser; creates a free account if you don't have one):

This is your checkout's deployment identity: every `fly` command and data script from here on reads its target from it, so nothing needs an app name on the command line anymore. `fly.toml` also holds the region and VM sizing — adjust `primary_region` to a region near you and commit:

Because each checkout manages exactly one app (see Your site is your repo), the target always comes from `fly.toml` — there's no app name to get wrong. If you ever do need to address a different app (say, a staging copy), every `fly` command and data script accepts `-a <app>` as an explicit override.

Editable's content-addressed assets send `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable`, so long-lived caching is safe. Do not cache pages or API routes. Turn off **Email Address Obfuscation** under **Security > Settings**, and be wary of any optimization that rewrites HTML or JavaScript, since changing SvelteKit's server-rendered output can break hydration.

The first run provisions the server — Docker, Caddy as the TLS-terminating reverse proxy, swap on machines with less than 2 GB RAM — asks you for an admin password, builds the Docker image locally, streams it over ssh, and starts the site. The server never needs access to your git repository or the memory to run a build. Your content lives in `/data` on the server — the same path Fly.io mounts and the same path inside the container; deploys replace the container and never touch that folder.

And every `pnpm data:*` command (Backup, sync & recovery) targets the VPS too (`fly.toml` is ignored; remove or comment `DEPLOY_HOST` to target Fly.io again). Pull, push, backups, restores, point-in-time recovery — the whole toolbox behaves the same, including disaster recovery from the backup bucket on a fresh volume.

`set` and `unset` restart the app and refresh the Caddy config, so the change takes effect immediately — no deploy needed, including for `ORIGIN` and `ALIAS_DOMAINS`. For automated backups, the `BUCKET_*` / `AWS_*` secrets belong in the server's `.env` — the first deploy copies them from your local `.env` if present; after that, changes are explicit via `vps:env`.

Arguments in brackets are optional; pnpm forwards them directly to the script, without an extra `--` separator. The cloud commands require Automated backups. Commands that connect to a deployment read the target app from `fly.toml`; only append `-a <app>` if no app name is set there, or to override it. Remote restores print a summary of the restored state (documents, last edited, assets). Both local and remote restores back up the state they replace first. `pnpm data:help` prints this reference, with arguments, in the terminal.

The database runs in SQLite WAL mode: recent writes live in a `db.sqlite3-wal` sidecar, not the main file. Copying the files of a running database loses or corrupts data. `data.sh` instead takes a consistent `VACUUM INTO` snapshot, which is safe even while the site is being edited. **Do not** back up by copying `data/` of a running instance.

A rollback restores only the database; it re-points at the same immutable asset pool, which is why `ASSET_GRACE_PERIOD_DAYS` (see Deploy) defines how far back you can safely go — restores from the backup bucket don't have this limit.

The manual snapshots above are deliberate actions you take. Optionally, Editable can also back itself up continuously to an S3-compatible bucket: the database is replicated on every write via Litestream (with point-in-time recovery), and uploaded assets are mirrored to the bucket as they arrive, with a reconciliation sweep at every boot catching anything missed. Everything is write-driven — there are no cron jobs, and suspend mode (`auto_stop_machines = "suspend"`) is fully supported: a suspended machine isn't writing anything, so there's nothing to miss. (One honest edge: replication ships changes on a ~1s interval, so a suspend arriving immediately after a write can hold the last segment in memory until the next wake — data is at risk only if the volume is destroyed before the machine ever wakes again, a seconds-wide window.)

* **Primary Programming Language**: **Golang v1.26.2** (Clean, efficient, and prioritizes pure performance).
* **API & HTTP Server**: **`net/http`** (Standard Library) & **`go-chi/chi/v5`** for lightweight, high-concurrency routing.
* **RPC Framework**: **`gRPC`** (`google.golang.org/grpc`) for fast, low-latency cross-service communication.
* **Message Broker (Event-Driven)**: **Kafka Client** via **`twmb/franz-go`** for feature-complete, high-performance asynchronous event streaming.
* **Payment Gateway Integration**: **`midtrans/midtrans-go`** as the official API client for managing secure checkout transactions and billing settlement.
* **Data Storage (Database)**: **MySQL 8.0** as an ACID-compliant transaction storage.

* **Database Interface**: **`database/sql`** (Standard Library) for native connection pooling and raw SQL execution (utilizing `PrepareCtx`, `BeginTx`, `QueryRowContext`, `QueryContext`, `ExecContext`).
* **Database Driver**: **`go-sql-driver/mysql`** for native interaction with the MySQL engine.
* **Data Validation**: **`go-playground/validator/v10`** for secure structural payload and input validation tags.
* **Image Processing Utility**: **`disintegration/imaging`** for image manipulation and upload management.
* **Testing Library**: **`Stretchr/Testify`** (`assert` & `mock`) for building isolated unit test architectures [index].
* **Auth Service**: Handles user authentication, credential verification, token generation (JWT), and authorization security across the platform.
* **User Service**: Manages customer profiles, account data structures, shipping addresses, and personal identification records.
* **Product Service**: Manages the global product catalog, regular inventory updates, and executes high-concurrency Flash Sale stock lock management.
* **Order Service**: Handles the complete checkout lifecycle, local order processing, idempotency tracking, and local outbox transaction logging.
* **Payment Service**: Manages interaction with payment gateways, processes billing transactions, and handles dynamic transaction invoices.
* **Notification Service**: Processes asynchronous customer communications (such as order confirmation emails via Kafka) driven by backend transaction workers.

* **Inter-Service Communication**: Leverages low-latency **gRPC** for internal synchronous network calls and the **Transactional Outbox Pattern** combined with a message broker for reliable asynchronous events.

Contains the fundamental business objects (`Order`, `Product`, `FlashSale`) and strict domain rules. This layer is written in pure Golang, has **zero dependencies** on any other layers or external libraries, and heavily utilizes *value types* instead of pointers to maximize stack allocation.

Orchestrates the specific business logic of the service (`CreateCheckout`, `DeductFlashSaleStock`). It interacts directly with the Domain layer and defines abstract interfaces (ports) for data access or external clients, completely unaware of *how* data is stored or fetched.

Implements the interfaces defined by the Use Case layer. This is where **`database/sql`** and **`go-sql-driver/mysql`** reside. It executes raw SQL queries, manages local ACID transactions via `db.BeginTx`, and maps relational database rows directly into domain value structures using `rows.Scan()`. Additionally, it heavily utilizes **`PrepareCtx`** to pre-compile SQL statements natively, maximizing execution speed and ensuring full protection against SQL injection during high-volume traffic.

The outermost gate handled by **`net/http`** (for client-facing REST APIs) and **`google.golang.org/grpc`** (for internal inter-service RPC communication). It parses payloads, decodes gRPC requests, runs entry-level validation, triggers the appropriate Use Case, and returns structured network responses.
1. **Ingress Request**: The client hits the API Gateway via HTTP, which parses the input into an immutable value struct and maps it to a gRPC client request.
2. **Local Isolation**: The Order Use Case coordinates internal business rules and commits the order alongside an outbox payload safely inside a local MySQL transaction block.

3. **Distributed Consistency**: The Outbox Worker polls the local transaction table asynchronously and synchronizes the state by invoking the downstream Product Service via gRPC to safely reduce physical catalog inventory.

* **Pure Pass-by-Value**: Data structures are passed across layer boundaries as explicit copies (`Product` instead of `*Product`) whenever feasible. This keeps the data scoped to the function execution block, ensuring it stays allocated on the **Stack** and prevents *Escape Analysis* from moving it to the **Heap**.

* **Boundary Decoupling via Interfaces**: Use Cases rely strictly on interfaces to communicate with Repositories. This decoupling allows **`Stretchr/Testify`** to inject lightweight mocks during unit testing, enabling full test coverage without needing network or database resources.

* **Explicit Resource Management**: Database rows and HTTP request bodies are closed immediately after consumption using native Go defer statements (`rows.Close()`, `r.Body.Close()`), ensuring deterministic memory cleanup without relying on the GC to release system descriptors.

* **Context:** Currently, the system isolates failures locally using database transactional rollbacks. As the ecosystem grows, complex multi-service workflows (such as matching a successful `Order` with a third-party `Payment` gateway deduction and an inventory commit in the `Product Service`) will require cross-network atomicity.

* **Evolution:** We plan to implement an **Orchestration-Based Saga Pattern**. A centralized coordinator inside the `Order Service` will manage successful steps via gRPC and fire explicit **Compensating Transactions** (such as releasing locked stock or triggering a refund) if a downstream payment execution fails mid-way.

* **Context:** Tracking down performance bottlenecks or hidden heap allocations across multiple network hops (Gateway -> gRPC Client -> gRPC Server -> MySQL) can become difficult using raw local terminal logs.

* **Evolution:** Integrating **OpenTelemetry** linked with **Jaeger** or **Grafana Tempo**. By propagating a unique `trace_id` inside the gRPC Metadata Context, we can visually map the exact latency and execution profile of a user’s checkout request across all network microservice boundaries in real-time.

* **Context:** The current `flash_sale_caches` table resides directly inside the relational `order_db` MySQL storage. While it protects the main transaction tables, a relational database disk I/O still has structural throughput limitations under millions of requests.

* **Evolution:** Introducing a distributed in-memory **Redis Cluster** equipped with **Lua Scripting** to handle atomic `DECRBY` check-and-deduct operations for Flash Sales. MySQL will then purely receive finalized, asynchronous bulk inserts from the Outbox Worker, pushing the system's concurrency boundaries even further.
